items.title: David Torkanowsky interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, September 26, 2019
items.q: One of their sons is Dean Baquet, the editor of the New York Times.

ctx.x: You were talking about people assuming or saying that it’s back to where it was.

Oh, I’m sorry, you’re right. So I wrote this scathing response saying that you know I mean listen, after Katrina happened the then-speaker of the house Denny Hastert actually said, “New Orleans is going to be too expensive to rebuild. If people want to hear jazz they can go to Walt Disney World.” Yeah he said that. The letter I wrote him I’m surprised I didn’t get a knock on the door from the Secret Service ‘cause it was pretty caustic. But the point is no, no, no. I mean here’s the thing. New Orleans — jazz was…

why music flourished in New Orleans, why the creativity? She said, that’s easy, leisure time. In New Orleans, I mean it’s not called “The Big Easy” for nothing. And you know you could always go by so-and-so mama’s house who got some gumbo on the stove and you could make zero dollars in New Orleans and eat just fine. So people hung out, they hung out with each other and they shedded and they created, you know, music, like Ellis Marsalis, the quintet, the early quintet. They — James Black. They influenced Coltrane…
